The iShares 10+ Year Investment Grade Corporate Bond ETF (NYSEMKT:IGLB) and State Street SPDR Portfolio Long Term Corporate Bond ETF (NYSEMKT:SPLB) provide nearly identical, low-cost exposure to long-dated investment-grade corporate debt.

Investors seeking long-term income and portfolio diversification often turn to corporate bond ETFs. Both the iShares and SPDR funds target high-quality corporate issues with maturities exceeding 10 years. While their portfolios overlap significantly, subtle differences in liquidity, scale, and diversification may influence an investor's preference.

What's inside

The iShares 10+ Year Investment Grade Corporate Bond ETF focuses on U.S. dollar-denominated, investment-grade corporate bonds with at least 10 years remaining until maturity. It is a large portfolio containing 3,815 holdings, and it is highly diversified, as its largest positions include no single issue exceeding 0.27% of assets. The fund was launched in 2009. The iShares 10+ Year Investment Grade Corporate Bond ETF has paid $2.61 per share over the trailing 12 months, which, on its recent ~$47.44 share price, works out to a 5.5% yield.

The State Street SPDR Portfolio Long Term Corporate Bond ETF likewise focuses on long-dated corporate issues by tracking the Bloomberg U.S. Long Term Corporate Bond Index. It is also highly diversified with 2,952 holdings, and its top holdings include no single position representing more than 0.47% of the portfolio assets. This fund was launched in 2009. The State Street SPDR Portfolio Long Term Corporate Bond ETF has paid $1.20 per share over the trailing 12 months, which on its recent ~$21.19 share price works out to a 5.6% yield.

title: S&P 500 Recovered $1 Trillion in 90 Minutes Despite Wider Market Crash
detail:
S&P 500 Recovered $1 Trillion in 90 Minutes Despite Wider Market Crash
Jakub Dziadkowiec
Thu, November 12, 2026 at 2:14 PM MST 2 min read
NVDA
^GSPC
AMD
AVGO
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The S&P 500 looked headed for a bruising Thursday after Nvidia lost as much as $600 billion in market value. Then Wall Street reversed course.

The index fell nearly 1% at the opening bell as Nvidia shares plunged up to 14% following founder Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation. Within about 90 minutes, the S&P 500 had recovered its losses.

Why Didn't Nvidia Drag Down the Whole Market?

Nvidia's sell-off was severe, but it eased as trading progressed. Buyers also moved into its competitors: AMD rose roughly 7%, while Broadcom gained more than 5%.

Gains elsewhere helped offset Nvidia's losses, suggesting investors were still willing to bet on demand for AI chips, even as they questioned Nvidia's leadership.

Retail investors bought an estimated $111 million of Nvidia shares in the first half-hour alone, Reuters reported.

"You notice some of Nvidia's losses have been offset by gains in competitors," Peter Tuz, president of Chase Investment Counsel, told Reuters.

Nvidia has appointed finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO. Its next earnings report on November 17 will test whether customers' spending and growth expectations can withstand the leadership upheaval.

What Should Stock Market Investors Watch Next?

The S&P 500 rebound happened despite another warning sign: the 10-year US Treasury yield climbed above 5%, making borrowing more expensive.

Oil prices also rose after President Donald Trump hardened his position on Iran, adding to inflation worries.

On the chart, the S&P 500's immediate challenge is holding above roughly 7,624. A sustained move higher would put its record near 7,845 back in sight.

If selling returns, 7,484 is the first level to watch, followed by the November low near 7,350.

S&P 500 daily chart. Source: TradingView

Thursday showed that investors still want to buy market dips. Whether that enthusiasm survives higher yields and Nvidia's first earnings report without Huang remains the bigger question.

We just published a list of the 10 Stocks Analysts Are Downgrading Right Now and Wix.com (NASDAQ:WIX) ranked 6th on this list.

Stocks slid again on Tuesday after a hotter-than-expected inflation report fed bets on higher interest rates, and all three major indexes finished lower. The Dow fell 0.30% to 52,231.89, the S&P 500 lost 0.38% to 7,520.93, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.74% to 25,065.87.

Government data showed consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, the third straight monthly gain of at least that size, against the 0.3% economists expected. Core prices rose 0.3%, ahead of a 0.2% forecast, and traders spent the session weighing how many more rate increases may be coming.

10 Unrivaled Stocks to Buy for the Next Decade

Photo by Arturo Añez on Unsplash

Rate-Hike Talk Hits a Market Already Under Strain

Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said the central bank should raise rates in December and consider a half-point increase, while Dallas Federal Reserve President Lorie Logan said at least two more quarter-point hikes are needed. Traders now see an 84% chance of a quarter-point move next month and a 15% chance of a half-point increase.

Jason Ware, chief investment officer at Albion Financial Group, told Reuters that investors are spooked by the possibility of a 50 basis point hike. That worry landed on a market that had already taken a beating: the Nasdaq closed nearly 12% below its October peak last week, and the S&P 500 sank 4.4% in a single session, its worst day since April 2025. For the other side of that debate, see our list of oversold AI stocks where Wall Street analysts see 50%+ upside.

Skyler Weinand, chief investment officer at Regan Capital, said stocks have seen a heavy rotation out of AI-related names and into defensive sectors such as healthcare. Technology took the sharpest hit. Last week the S&P 500 technology sector fell 7.3% and the Philadelphia semiconductor index dropped more than 12% as fears of a data-center slowdown spread after the midterm elections.

Oxford Economics expects the Fed to raise rates in December and again in March, while Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid described policy as still accommodative.

Wix made it to our list because it drew an analyst downgrade on November 10 and has an average upside potential of 16%. Bank of America analyst Michael McGovern downgraded Wix to Underperform from Buy on November 10 and cut his price target to $68 from $75. He cites slowing growth in Partners, the business where agencies build sites for clients, competition from AI coding tools such as Lovable and Cursor, and higher marketing spending that could limit profit. He says rapid growth at Base44, Wix's AI app-building platform, is masking weaker underlying performance.

title: How Much Downside Is Left In Caterpillar Stock?
detail:
How Much Downside Is Left In Caterpillar Stock?
Trefis Team
Thu, November 12, 2026 at 2:29 PM MST 3 min read
CAT
^GSPC
DE
PCAR
CMI
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Caterpillar (CAT) stock lost 22% in the month to November 11, while the S&P 500 slipped 2.3%. That leaves the shares 43.3% below their highest close of the past year, set on June 30. If the rest of the market falls as well, how hard could that hit Caterpillar, judging by past market shocks?

How Far Has Caterpillar Fallen In Market Shocks?

Caterpillar stock dropped an average of 23.4% during the 15 market shocks since 2007, compared with a 15.8% decline for the S&P 500 over the same windows. The stock fell further than the index during most of those shocks. The largest of those declines came during the 2008-2009 financial crisis, when Caterpillar lost 69% and the S&P 500 lost 53%.

One shock on that list barely moved the broader market but hit Caterpillar hard. During the oil price slump of 2014 to 2016, Caterpillar lost 44% while the S&P 500 fell 6.8%.

The median recovery took 2.5 months from the low. Four of those recoveries stretched beyond a year, however, with the slowest taking 37.3 months following the summer 2007 credit crunch. The stock returned to its earlier peak after every one of those shocks.

Caterpillar's Sales Are Growing Faster Than A Year Ago

Caterpillar's revenue rose 20.3% in the twelve months to September 30, 2026, following a 1.5% decline in the twelve months before. In fiscal 2025, Power & Energy revenue rose 11.6%, while Construction Industries revenue slipped 1.6%. In the third quarter of 2026, management said Construction Industries sales grew 18% to $8 billion and Power & Energy sales grew 18% to $8.8 billion.

Caterpillar also kept more of each dollar of sales. Its operating margin reached 18.3% over the latest twelve months, up from 17.7% a year earlier. The company holds more debt than it did, however, carrying $45.2 billion on September 30, 2026, compared with $41.5 billion a year earlier.

Where Is Caterpillar Under Pressure Now?

On its October 29 earnings call, management said it expects dealers to cut their inventory by roughly $1.6 billion in the fourth quarter. Management called this the typical seasonal cut, though it is larger than the $600 million cut a year earlier, and management put the year-over-year hit to fourth-quarter sales volume.

Management also pointed to costs. The company expects tariff costs of around $2.2 billion for 2026, excluding the tariff recoveries it has received so far. Those tariffs, higher freight costs and spending on new capacity are why management expects its adjusted operating margin for the year, leaving out tariff recoveries, to sit near the bottom of its target range.
